summary: This informational RFC is part of a series on using modern cryptographic mechanisms for message authentication in routing protocols (KARP). It defines a framework for a key management protocol that could create and manage session keys for authentication and integrity.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers talk to each other and need secret handshakes. This is a plan for how to hand out and change those secret handshakes safely.

questions: keying and authentication for routing protocols
why use a key management protocol for routers
subtitle: A roadmap for adding modern message authentication and key management to routing protocols.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols exchange messages between neighboring routers, and many rely on old, mostly manually keyed authentication. Attacks on the core routing infrastructure can cause maximal disruption at minimal cost.
tldr.mechanism: The KARP work sorts routing protocols into categories, then improves each protocol's authentication in two phases: first modern algorithms and key agility with manual keys, then an automated key management protocol (KMP). Keys reach routing protocols through a protocol-independent key table abstraction.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational design-guidelines document, not a protocol specification. It gives design teams a roadmap, a gap-analysis checklist and security cautions.

today: RFC 6518 is an Informational document from February 2012 and is not marked as obsoleted or updated in the metadata for this site. It is guidance for KARP design teams, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Scope: Securing Packets on the Wire
sections.content:
In March 2006 the Internet Architecture Board held a workshop on unwanted Internet traffic, reported in RFC 4948. It called the core routing infrastructure an ideal attack target of minimal cost but maximal disruption and listed four steps to tighten it. This document addresses the last one: securing the routing protocols' packets on the wire between directly communicating peers. Checking that routing information is properly authorized is a separate matter and out of scope.

KARP (Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols) centers on a key table abstraction. When a routing protocol sends or receives a message, it looks up the key in this table, and automated key management fills the table when keys become available. Implementations are not required to use this abstraction; it serves standardization and management.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is to make sure the messages routers pass to each other cannot be faked, using a shared key lookup that routers consult each time.

sections.title: Categorizing Routing Protocols
sections.content:
Protocols are grouped by two attributes so that design teams can reuse authentication mechanisms.

By message transaction type: one-to-one (BGP, LDP, BFD, RSVP-TE), one-to-many on a link (OSPF and IS-IS in broadcast mode, RIP) and multicast (PIM-SM, which also has some unicast messages to a Rendezvous Point).

By keying: peer keying, where a uniquely keyed security association is set up between two routers, and group keying, where one keying message serves many peers and a group security association is used. Ideally one key management protocol is created per category.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers talk to one friend, some shout to a whole room, and each kind needs a different way to share the secret.

sections.title: Key Management and the Key Life Cycle
sections.content:
Even for manually keyed work, designers must think ahead to a future KMP and what it would hand to a routing protocol: a security association identifier (such as an IPsec SPI or the TCP-AO KeyID), a key lifetime, the algorithms, the keys and their direction. RFC 4107 should be consulted when designing a reusable KMP model.

Asymmetric keys generated on the router and never moved off it need not be changed when an administrator leaves, and being random they resist dictionary attacks. Keys should have limited lifetimes. A key chain does not help if the routing stack cannot roll to new keys without bouncing sessions, so the first step is to fix the stack. The RFC also notes that frequent manual key changes can increase exposure, since keys are most likely to be disclosed while being changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Secret passwords should be swapped now and then, but swapping them badly can make things worse. The routers must be able to switch without hanging up on each other.

sections.title: The Two-Phase Roadmap
sections.content:
Phase 1 enhances each protocol's current authentication to modern, consistent security within its existing, largely manual key management. Creating or embedding a KMP is explicitly excluded. Teams characterize the protocol, define the optimal state, do a gap analysis, plan transition and deployment (do adjacencies need to bounce?), and assign the design work.

Phase 2 develops an automated key management framework giving unique pair-wise (or group-wise) keys per peering. A KMP provides fresh traffic keys for each session, which helps prevent inter-connection replay attacks, negotiates algorithms and lifetimes, and rekeys before expiry without administrator action. The key management protocol should be clearly separated from the routing transport, which stays oblivious to how keys are derived.

Each protocol gets its own team. The RFC expects manual and automated key management to coexist in the real world, and says simplicity and deployability are the keys to success.
sections.plainLanguage: Step one: give the routers better locks. Step two: add a helper that hands out and changes the keys automatically.

sections.title: Protocol Groups, Incremental Deployment and DoS
sections.content:
The RFC places protocols in groups. BGP, LDP, PCEP and MSDP are one-to-one with peer keying; most use TCP, so work on TCP-AO (RFC 5925) applies, though TCP-AO cannot protect LDP's UDP discovery exchanges. OSPF, IS-IS and RIP use group keying. BFD gets its own team because of its millisecond timers and sequence number rollover. RSVP and RSVP-TE use a keyed digest per hop; KARP will work only on RSVP-TE. PIM-SM and PIM-DM are grouped together.

New mechanisms must support incremental deployment and backward compatibility in a mixed environment, because they cannot be deployed everywhere at once. They also must not open denial-of-service holes: a device should never have to try several keys on an incoming packet, and cheap checks such as the IP header check in RFC 5082 can limit which packets get cryptographic validation. Replays by an outsider should not be able to disrupt routing sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can be upgraded one at a time, and the new locks must not be so heavy that a bully can tire a router out by knocking over and over.

sections.title: Gap Analysis and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Design teams review the threats and requirements document, then check each requirement for their protocol: at least one mandatory modern algorithm, a default algorithm set accepted by the community, algorithm agility, rekeying without disrupting routing, and replay protection within and between connections. They also weigh processing cost, since most deployed routers lack cryptographic hardware accelerators.

On keys, the RFC advises unpredictable keys (RFC 4086) and different keys per peer where possible. When manual keys are used, a pre-shared key should go through a key derivation function mixed with connection-specific material, which gives peer-unique traffic keys and replay protection. It recommends running cryptographic authentication on all adjacencies, starting from the outside in: EBGP links before IBGP links. Using a group key may be acceptable on an internal link, while pair-wise keys suit a public exchange point.
sections.plainLanguage: Use hard-to-guess secrets, a different one for each friend, and protect the outside doors first.
